subject: Agriculture
title: Vertical Integration in Poultry
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: Vertical Integration in Poultry.

hook.text: Most US chicken farmers don't own their chickens. Companies own the birds and pay farmers to raise them.

buildup.text: Tyson, Perdue, and other firms control breeding, feed, processing, and marketing. Farmers just provide labor and barns.

discovery.text: This tournament system ranks farmers against each other. Bottom performers get fewer chicks—or get cut entirely.

twist.text: Contract farmers carry hundreds of thousands in debt for their barns but have almost no bargaining power.

climax.text: Vertical integration made chicken cheap for consumers but trapped farmers in a system they can't escape.

punchline.text: The farmer raises the birds. The company makes the rules.

quiz.question: What is vertical integration in the poultry industry?
options: A few companies controlling breeding, feed, processing, and marketing

details.summary: Vertical integration in poultry means a single company controls every stage—from breeding and feed to processing and retail. This topic covers how this model revolutionized chicken production, lowered prices, and concentrated power over contract farmers.
details.whyItMatters: Vertical integration made chicken the cheapest meat in many countries but left contract growers with little negotiating power, slim margins, and heavy debt for company-mandated equipment upgrades.
takeaways: Four companies control over 50% of US chicken processing capacity
Contract farmers own the buildings and debt while companies own the birds and feed
Vertical integration cut US chicken prices by over 50% in real terms since 1960

faq.question: How does vertical integration work in the poultry industry?
faq.answer: An integrator company owns the hatcheries, feed mills, and processing plants. Contract growers raise company-owned birds in grower-owned facilities, following strict company protocols. The company sets pay based on performance rankings among its growers.

faq.question: Why is vertical integration controversial for farmers?
faq.answer: Growers invest hundreds of thousands of dollars in facilities but have little bargaining power. Companies can terminate contracts, demand expensive upgrades, and rank growers against each other—creating a system many farmers describe as modern serfdom.
